questions.question: What are ActiveRecord validations and how do you use them?
questions.title: ActiveRecord Validations Basics
questions.direct_answer: Validations are rules that ensure only valid data is saved: validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true, validates :age, numericality: { greater_than: 0 }. They run before save and create; if any fail, save and create return false and the record isn't persisted, and errors are added to record.errors. They're how you keep bad data out of the database at the model layer — one source of truth, checked on every save, instead of checking in the controller or the database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know validates with presence/uniqueness/numericality, that they run before save (return false on fail), and errors land on record.errors.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Validating in the controller instead of the model (duplicated, easy to miss), or not checking save's return.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: validates :field, presence/uniqueness/numericality run before save; save/create return false and errors land on record.errors if they fail.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define ActiveRecord Validations Basics simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Rules That Run Before Save
sections.content: Validations are rules that ensure only valid data is saved. You declare them in the model: validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true; validates :age, numericality: { greater_than: 0 }; validates :name, length: { minimum: 2 }. They run before save and create; if any fail, save and create return false and the record isn't persisted, and the failing checks are added to record.errors (you can show them with record.errors.full_messages). They're how you keep bad data out of the database at the model layer — one source of truth, checked on every save, instead of checking in the controller or the database separately.

sections.title: Save With Validations
sections.content:
validates run before save; on failure save returns false and errors are set.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[save called] --> V[validates run]
  V -->|pass| DB[row written]
  V -->|fail| E[save returns false; errors set]
```

sections.title: Validations and checking them
sections.content:
```ruby
class User < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true
  validates :age, numericality: { greater_than: 0 }
  validates :name, length: { minimum: 2 }
end

u = User.new(name: 'A', age: -1)        # name too short, age negative
u.save                                   # false (not persisted)
u.errors.full_messages                   # ['Name is too short', 'Age must be greater than 0']
u.valid?                                 # false

# Use save! to raise on failure instead of returning false:
u.save!   # raises ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid
```

sections.title: Common Validators
rows: No other row has the same value

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Validating in the controller instead of the model — duplicated and easy to miss.
Not checking save's return (false) — the record silently isn't persisted.
Confusing save (returns false) with save! (raises) — pick by intent.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Validations are rules that ensure only valid data is saved, declared in the model.
validates :field, presence/uniqueness/numericality/length run before save and create.
On failure, save and create return false (or save! raises) and errors go on record.errors.
Validations are the model-layer source of truth — one place, checked on every save.
Use valid? to check without saving; errors.full_messages to read the failures.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Validations are rules that ensure only valid data is saved. You declare them in the model: validates of email, presence true and uniqueness true; validates of age, numericality of greater_than zero; validates of name, length of minimum two. They run before save and create; if any fail, save and create return false and the record isn't persisted, and the failing checks are added to record.errors, which you can show with errors.full_messages. They're how you keep bad data out of the database at the model layer — one source of truth, checked on every save, instead of checking in the controller or the database separately. A common mistake is validating in the controller instead of the model, which is duplicated and easy to miss, and not checking save's return, because the record silently isn't persisted. Use valid to check without saving and save bang to raise on failure.
